title: QEMScore: How Much Does the Measurement Add to Learned Quantum Error Mitigation?
authors: Yue Zhao, Huayue Gu, Yushun Dong, Xiyang Hu
abstract: How much does the noisy measurement add to learned quantum error mitigation? An accuracy table cannot say, because a model handed circuit structure can score well without reading the measurement at all. QEMScore adds the comparison that can. Each simulated circuit carries an exact ideal answer. The learned mitigator is scored beside a capacity-matched control, a model just as flexible that reads the same circuit description but never the measurement. Each method's measurement spend is accounted and not equalized. We run a controlled campaign on simulated circuits and reanalyze two published learned mitigators, Q-LEAR and QRAFT, from their released hardware data. Three findings stand out. First, under familiar within-family conditions (S0) evaluated across two spin-chain families and three seeds, continuous couplings identify the target, and the control that never reads the measurement matches 87.7 to 100.5 percent of the mitigator's gain over an affine fit to the circuit description. A plain polynomial in the coupling parameters, fitted after the campaign, beats the mitigator on all six evaluations, reflecting the selected learners' capacity. Second, for these selected learners, matching most of the gain is not matching the accuracy: on five of six evaluations the mitigator removes 19.5 to 74.5 percent of the error the capacity-matched control leaves, a learner-specific gap rather than a measurement requirement. Third, on released hardware data where descriptors only partially identify queries, the findings differ: flexible models of the descriptors show negligible mean gain over affine fits in Q-LEAR, and measurement inputs carry predictive gains in both Q-LEAR and QRAFT. These comparisons reflect representation- and protocol-specific behavior rather than an isolated cross-regime difference. A learned mitigator's accuracy should therefore be reported beside such controls.
summary: This paper introduces QEMScore, a diagnostic framework to quantify the specific contribution of noisy measurement outcomes to the performance of learned quantum error mitigation techniques. By comparing full models against controls that ignore measurement data, the authors show that while measurement matters, the mitigation gain can stem from other sources, necessitating more nuanced reporting standards in the field.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental question of how much of the performance gain in learned quantum error mitigation (QEM) techniques is attributable to the noisy measurement input versus the circuit structure itself.
main_result: The measurement-only control can account for a significant portion of the mitigator's gain under controlled conditions, and on actual hardware data, measurement inputs do carry predictive gains.
method: A novel framework, QEMScore, is introduced to compare learned mitigators against capacity-matched controls that are explicitly prevented from reading the measurement outcome, allowing for the quantification of the measurement's contribution.
model_or_system: The study uses simulated quantum circuits, including spin-chain families (e.g., transverse-field Ising), and evaluates observables $\langle O angle$ under various noise models and measurement protocols.
key_observables: Error reduction quantified by the measurement-associated gap ($D = C - F$), and the share ($S$) of error reduction attributed to the measurement input.
important_parameters: The analysis is highly dependent on the specific simulated circuit regimes, the noise configuration, and the computational budget used for the learned models.
main_assumptions: The conclusions are strictly conditional on the tested simulator regimes and the specific comparison controls implemented; the measurement contribution is not always the sole source of mitigation gain.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the comparison framework, showing how the full model's performance is decomposed into components related to circuit features and measurement readings. Other figures detail the comparison across various evaluation settings (S0-S6).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the scientific problem by noting the ambiguity in current error mitigation reporting. It then introduces the QEMScore framework, details controlled simulations on spin-chain families, presents quantitative results comparing different control models, and concludes with guidelines for reporting learned mitigator accuracy.
why_interesting: It provides rigorous diagnostic tools for assessing the true physical utility of complex machine learning models applied to quantum computation, helping researchers distinguish between genuine physical insight and mere correlation with measurement noise.
